paragraphs: “How can you know that? How can you talk so sure of yourself?” Alyosha asked sharply, with a frown.
“Why do you ask, and why does my answer scare you? It shows you know I’m telling the truth.”
“You don’t like Ivan. Ivan wouldn’t be tempted by money.”
“Wouldn’t he? And what about Katerina Ivanovna’s beauty? It isn’t only the money, though sixty thousand is an attraction.”
“Ivan is above that. He wouldn’t court anyone for thousands. Money isn’t what Ivan is after, nor comfort. Perhaps what he’s after is suffering.”
“What wild dream is that? Oh, you—aristocrats!”
“Ah, Misha, his spirit is stormy. His mind is held in bondage. A great unsolved doubt haunts him. He is one of those who don’t want millions, but an answer to their questions.”

“That’s plagiarism, Alyosha. You’re quoting your elder’s phrases. Ah, so Ivan has set you a problem!” cried Rakitin, with open malice. His face changed and his lips twitched. “And a stupid problem it is. It’s no use guessing at it. Rack your brains and you’ll understand it. His article is absurd and ridiculous. And did you hear his stupid theory just now? If there’s no immortality of the soul, there’s no virtue, and everything is lawful. (And by the way, remember how your brother Mitya cried out: ‘I will remember!’) A charming theory for scoundrels!—(I’m being abusive, which is stupid.) Not for scoundrels, but for pedantic _poseurs_, ‘haunted by profound, unsolved doubts.’ He’s showing off, and it all boils down to ‘on the one hand we cannot but admit’ and ‘on the other it must be confessed!’ His whole theory is a fraud! Humanity will find the power to live for virtue within itself, even without believing in immortality. It will find it in love of freedom, of equality, of fraternity.”
Rakitin could hardly contain himself in his heat, but all at once, as if he had remembered something, he broke off.
“Well, that’s enough,” he said, with a smile twisted still further. “What are you laughing at? Do you take me for a vulgar fool?”

“No, it never crossed my mind to take you for a vulgar fool. You’re clever, but ... never mind, it was silly of me to smile. I understand why you get so hot about it, Misha. From your warmth I guess you’re not indifferent to Katerina Ivanovna yourself. I’ve suspected it for a long time, brother, and that’s why you dislike my brother Ivan. Are you jealous of him?”
“Jealous of her money, too? Won’t you add that?”
“I won’t say a word about money. I’m not going to insult you.”

“I believe you, since you say so, but the devil take you, and your brother Ivan with you. Can’t you see a man might dislike him quite apart from Katerina Ivanovna? And why the devil should I like him? He condescends to abuse me, you know. Why shouldn’t I abuse him?”
“I’ve never heard him say anything about you, good or bad. He doesn’t mention you at all.”

“Well, I heard that the day before yesterday, at Katerina Ivanovna’s, he abused me for all he was worth. That shows what an interest he takes in your humble servant. And which of us is the jealous one after that, brother, I can’t say. He was so kind as to give his opinion that if I don’t take up the career of an archimandrite in the near future and become a monk, I’m sure to go to Petersburg and get on some solid magazine as a reviewer. I’ll write for it ten years, he says, and in the end become the owner of the magazine and publish it on the liberal and atheistic side, with a socialistic tinge, a tiny gloss of socialism, but keeping a sharp lookout all the while, that is, keeping in with both sides and fooling the fools. By your brother’s account, the tinge of socialism won’t prevent me from putting the profits aside and investing them under the guidance of some Jew, until at the end of my career I build a great house in Petersburg, move my publishing offices into it, and rent the upper floors to lodgers. He has even picked the spot, near the new stone bridge over the Neva, which they say is going to be built in Petersburg.”
“Ah, Misha, that’s exactly what will happen, every word of it,” cried Alyosha, who could not hold back a good-humored smile.
“So you’re pleased to be sarcastic, too, Alexey Fyodorovitch.”

“No, no, I’m joking, forgive me. I’m thinking of something quite different. But excuse me, who can have told you all this? You can’t have been at Katerina Ivanovna’s yourself when he was talking about you?”

“I wasn’t there, but Dmitri Fyodorovitch was, and I heard him tell it with my own ears. If you must know, he didn’t tell me. I overheard him, without meaning to, of course, because I was sitting in Grushenka’s bedroom and couldn’t get away, with Dmitri Fyodorovitch in the next room.”
“Oh, yes, I forgot that she’s a relation of yours.”
“A relation! Grushenka, a relation of mine!” cried Rakitin, turning crimson. “Have you gone mad? You’re out of your mind!”
“Why, isn’t she a relation of yours? So I was told.”

“Where on earth did you hear that? You Karamazovs brag about being an ancient, noble family, though your father used to run around playing the buffoon at other men’s tables and was let into the kitchen only as a favor. I may be only a priest’s son, and dirt in the eyes of noblemen like you, but don’t insult me so lightly and so wantonly. I have a sense of honor, too, Alexey Fyodorovitch. I couldn’t be a relation of Grushenka, a common harlot. Kindly get that into your head!”
Rakitin was thoroughly irritated.

“Forgive me, for heaven’s sake, I had no idea ... besides ... how can you call her a harlot? Is she ... that kind of woman?” Alyosha suddenly flushed. “I tell you again, I heard she was a relation of yours. You go to see her often, and you told me yourself that you’re not her lover. I never dreamed that you, of all people, felt such contempt for her! Does she really deserve it?”

“I may have my own reasons for visiting her. That’s none of your business. As for relationship, your brother, or even your father, is more likely to make her your relation than mine. Well, here we are. You’d better go to the kitchen. Hello! What’s the matter, what is it? Are we late? They can’t have finished dinner so soon! Have the Karamazovs been making trouble again? Of course they have. Here’s your father, and your brother Ivan after him. They’ve burst out of the Father Superior’s. And look, Father Isidor is shouting something after them from the steps. Your father’s shouting back and waving his arms. Cursing, I expect. Bah, and there goes Miüsov, driving off in his carriage. You see, he’s leaving. And old Maximov is running!—there must have been a row. There can’t have been any dinner. Surely they haven’t beaten the Father Superior! Or were they beaten themselves, maybe? It would serve them right!”
Rakitin’s cries had good cause. A scandalous, unheard-of scene had taken place. It had all sprung from the impulse of a moment.
